reason: Correct permit rule, but extraneous detail and a loosely paraphrased certificate condition.
Correctly identifies qualified-person supervision and supports the related duties with citations.
Correct core answer, but human-body material distracts and an inference lacks direct support.
Direct and supported explanation of written directions for infected-animal articles.
Correctly identifies the Collector. The full passage supports the answer, although its preview is truncated.

Correctly states the Record of Apportionment of Rents book and that the Collector records under his hand all particulars furnished or determined under the Act (s 9(1)); the extra s 9(2) prima facie evidence point is supported by the cited text.
Correctly says the Minister appoints any registered architect to fill the vacancy as soon as practicable (s 4E(4)); fully supported by CTX1.

Correctly identifies the Board as approving the seal device and able to break, change, alter or remake the seal (s 5(1)); supported by CTX1. DS2/DS3 are identical provisions of other Acts, not the Architects Act.

Directly answers that records need not be on paper because s 6(3) lets the Chief Surveyor keep them in electronic media or other means. The many further bullets on deposit, evidence and ETA rules are accurate to the passages but are distracting padding.

Correctly leads with the owner duty to preserve boundary marks under s 10(1). The later sections on repair costs, offences, parks and State land are supported by the passages but go well beyond the question.
Correctly gives a term not exceeding 3 years specified by the Minister and confirms reappointment is permitted (s 6(1)); fully supported by CTX1.
Correctly states that if both the Chairperson and Deputy Chairperson are absent the members present elect one of their number to preside (s 7(2)); supported by CTX1.

Correctly says the application is lodged in writing with an authorised nominating body (s 13). Added points on prior written notice, the 7-day limit and referral to an adjudicator are supported by CTX3 and CTX4 and bear on lodging.
Correctly states the trust account requirement (s 28A(1)) and accurately adds the account title wording, interest, withdrawal and ring-fencing rules from s 28A(2)-(6), all supported by CTX1.
Correctly identifies the developer as applicant and the Commissioner of Building Control as recipient (s 5(1)); fully supported by CTX1.

Correctly says the appropriate qualified person appointed under s 8 or 11 must appoint at least one site supervisor for the critical structural elements of small-scale works (s 10(2)); fully supported by CTX1.

Gives the licensed-bank deposit rule but never states that the fund must not be invested: it only says a managing agent has no power to invest and notes the supplied s 17(4) text cuts off at "must no". The reference answer is a flat no-investment rule. Claims are supported and the truncation is flagged honestly, but the extra management-fund investment point is a distraction.

Correctly answers yes under s 28(2) and lists the s 28(3) steps and offence. It wrongly places the 7-day deadline on all three steps, though only the notification and written-notice steps carry it; the apply-to-amend step has no stated deadline.

Leans towards yes but treats the missing reportable facility as insufficient by itself. The reference gives a direct entitlement (s 9(4)) when no reportable facility remains registered; the answer never identifies it because the supplied s 9 text was truncated. It applies s 10(4) discharge-of-liabilities limits, which are supported, but the claim that s 9 expressly gives the right is only inferred.

Correctly names the appellant and the Agency and limits appeals to questions of law or mixed law and fact (s 37(1)). The definitions are supported by the text. It omits the s 37(2) small-tax-change exception, which was not asked for.

Correctly answers yes to the licence and conditions requirement (s 7(1)) and the penalty in s 7(4) is supported. The extra material on consignment permits, licence applications and Food Safety and Security Act action is accurate to the cited text but goes beyond the question.

Does not give a clean answer. It names the "Agency" under the Food Safety and Security Act 2025 (s 210-211) as the current decision-maker without identifying it, and mentions the Control of Plants Act s 12 application to the Director-General only as the "previous route". The reference answer is the Director-General under s 12(1); since the supplied text shows FSSA provisions replacing that regime, the reference may be outdated. The claims are supported, but the answer is long and padded with vector-control material.
Correctly says the Director-General (of Public Health) keeps the register under s 9(1) and decides its form. The inspection right and the s 7(6) registration-record point are supported.

Correctly says a person must not create or permit conditions favourable to the propagation or harbouring of vectors (s 15(1)), with the s 15(4) presumption and s 15(2) directions. The opening retrieval-confidence caveat and the s 16, EPHA s 44 and s 48 material are supported but distracting.

Correctly quotes s 4(2): the court makes such order as seems just and orders how and by whom costs are borne. The "mandatory costs order" gloss follows from the text. The s 74(6) and s 74(3)-(4) points are accurate.

Correctly states a mortgagor in possession may grant an agricultural or occupation lease of up to 3 years (s 23(1)). The qualifications on contrary intention (s 23(11)), the 12-month rule (s 23(4)) and the rent and covenant requirements are supported by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 21(2) lets the sheriff follow and seize such property discovered in the course of removal without an order. The s 21(1) context is accurately described.
Correctly states that if no application is made within 10 days the sheriff must put the landlord in possession and the tenancy is deemed determined (s 23(2)); fully supported by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 3(2) lets the Authority authorise any person to assist, generally or in a particular case; fully supported by CTX1.
Correctly says the Authority determines the form, period, terms and conditions of every licence (s 10(2)). The listed example conditions from s 10(3) are supported by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 3(2) lets the Authority authorise any person to assist, generally or in a particular case; verbatim support in CTX1.

Correctly identifies the Authority as able to issue or approve codes of practice and standards of performance for the electricity industry (s 16(1)). The note that a code of practice includes a standard of performance is a modest addition drawn from CTX1.

Correctly answers no: under s 13(3) neither a supplier registration nor registered-goods registration is transferable without the Director-General's written approval; the definition of registered goods is supported by the cited s 10.
Correctly says the Director-General keeps the register and determines the particulars entered (s 14(1)); supported verbatim by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 4(1) requires a common seal that may be broken, altered or made anew as the Authority thinks fit; supported by CTX1. DS2-DS5 are parallel provisions of other statutes.
Correctly states the restriction that loans may be raised only in accordance with s 12 (s 12(1)), and accurately lists the s 12(2)-(3) methods and sources; all supported by CTX1.

Correctly identifies the occupier as the duty-holder under s 10(1), with s 10(2)-(3) and the definitions supported by the text. The s 13 owner/occupier notice paragraph and the definitions go beyond the question.

Correctly answers no: s 22(1) bars importing or offering a hazardous substance for sale without a Director-General licence, with the s 22(2), s 23 and Poisons Act points supported. The extra material about licence conditions and the Poisons Act is more than the question needs.
Correctly answers yes: s 13(3) makes both owner and occupier guilty of an offence where land is manured with nightsoil or human excreta, and s 13(1) prohibits it; supported by CTX1.
Correctly gives 12 hours in aggregate (s 21A(2)). The non-concurrent hours rule, Minister's Gazette power, 12-month period and 3-hour daily limit are all supported by s 21A(3), (6) and s 21B.
Correctly answers yes: s 7(1) requires a common seal that may be broken, changed, altered or made anew as the Council thinks fit; verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly says copies of the annual and supplementary estimates go to the Minister without delay upon adoption by the Council (s 18(1)); supported by CTX1.
Correctly states the register holds the names and prescribed particulars of registered inspectors (s 5(1)) and accurately notes s 5 does not itself set out the particulars.

Correctly states s 6(1): the application must be made in the prescribed manner with prescribed documents and particulars. The s 6(2)-(3) qualification and character points are supported, and it honestly notes the details sit in regulations.

Correctly says the aggrieved person may appeal to the Minister, whose decision is final (s 6(3) Fisheries Act), and s 6(4) excludes court proceedings; supported by CTX4. DS1-DS3 and DS5 are parallel appeal provisions of other statutes.
Correctly answers no: s 7(1) makes a fisheries licence valid only for the period, place or purpose specified; verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly identifies section 25 as governing the determination of quantity or average quantity (s 23(5)) and summarises the s 25(2) factors accurately from the cited text.

Correctly says the Director-General, Food Security must cancel the trigger notice on being satisfied the entity has permanently or indefinitely stopped all MSR activities (s 24(2)), and that the entity then ceases to be subject to the requirement (s 24(1)); supported by CTX1.
Correctly says a person whose property is damaged may appeal to the Minister whose decision is final (s 7(2)); the officer-inquiry point reflects s 7(3).

Correctly states the limitation: the President may lease only where declared not to create a substantial infringement of public rights (s 9(1)). The gazette notice, objections, purpose and mineral reservation points are supported by s 9(3)-(4) but go beyond the question.
Correctly answers yes: s 3(2) lets the Authority authorise any person to assist, generally or in a particular case; verbatim support in CTX1.

Mostly wrong against the reference, which says a gas transport agent's licence must not be granted to a gas retailer, gas shipper or town gas producer (s 7(7)). The answer says retailers and shippers "potentially" can hold one, reasoning from absence of a stated bar in the retrieved text (s 7(7) was not retrieved). Only the town gas producer answer is right in effect, via s 7(11), which is the converse provision. Its statements about the supplied text are honest and hedged.
Correctly answers yes: s 24(1) allows regulations to prescribe fees for applications and notices. The s 24(2)-(5) consequences and the s 48(1) power are accurately reported.

Correctly states s 25(3): a person authorised by an order under Part 3 regulations must not import or deal with the waste except in accordance with the order. The s 25(1)(b)-(c) and s 25(4) penalty details are supported by CTX1.
Correctly answers no under s 5(1) Hotels Act 1954. The registration process, s 6 conditions, s 16 penalties, licensing and exemption points are supported but go beyond the question.

Correctly answers yes: s 7(1) bars keeping or managing premises as a hotel unless one holds a valid licence granted in respect of those premises. The inference that another premises' licence does not suffice follows from that wording; the s 5 and s 12 points are supported.
Correctly answers yes and quotes s 4(1) accurately. The long summary of execution formalities in s 4(2)-(4) is accurate to CTX1 but unnecessary for the question.
Correctly states that the Board itself has the exclusive right to use the symbol or representation it selects (s 13(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.

Correctly answers no: s 4(1) prohibits housing development unless the developer holds a written Controller licence. The point that s 6 consent for using "housing developer" does not replace the licence is supported by CTX4.

Correctly lists the reportable matters under s 12(1): proposed sale or disposal of the business (including by amalgamation) and any reconstruction proposal. The Controller approval and offence points follow s 12(2) and (4).
Correctly says the Minister's approval governs interest rate and times and the mode and time of principal repayment (s 13(2)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly says s 17(2) applies the s 16 procedure to a supplemental budget and accurately summarises s 16(1)-(3) from the cited text.

Correct on the law: every witness examined by the Board is bound to state the truth and produce documents, on oath or not (s 25(5)). However, the supplied s 25 passage is cut off at "(5", so that holding is not visible in the retrieved text; only the s 25(4) summoning and production powers are supported.

Correctly answers no: where the Board is not constituted by the Commissioner alone, the Commissioner is not bound by the other members' advice or opinion (s 27(1)). The s 27(2)-(3) additions are supported.

Correctly states each joint owner is jointly and severally liable (s 18(1)). The contribution rights under s 34 are supported, but the apportionment between material interests (s 17) is a distraction from joint-owner liability.

Correctly says the outstanding charge can be recovered from any one or more of the responsible trustees (s 19(2)), and the s 19(3) definition of responsible trustees is accurate; both supported by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 7(2) lets the Collector postpone a sale and notify the postponed sale in the manner he sees fit; supported verbatim by CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 18(2) says the General Division of the High Court's order shall be final. The note about the consolidated version in force from 1 April 2022 matches the context header.
Correctly states a term not exceeding 2 years, reappointment possible and removal by the Minister at any time (s 4(3)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly says the president determines when and where the Board meets (s 5(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.

Correctly states that an entitled person lodges a primary application with the Registrar together with any deed, conveyance or instrument (s 20(1)). Entitled persons, form, evidence, mortgagor consent and corporate-applicant points are supported by s 20(2)-(6), and the certificate of correctness by s 59.

Correctly answers yes: s 21(1) lets the Registrar bring land in a conveyance registered under the Registration of Deeds Act under the Act if he or she thinks fit. The s 21(2)-(7) steps and definitions are supported.

Correctly states that the Registrar certifies the share in the common property in the subsidiary strata certificate and that no such certificate issues for the common property (s 13(2)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly answers no under s 15(1). The s 15(2)-(4) offence, nullity and cancellation points and the s 3 definitions are supported but go beyond the question.

Correctly identifies both landlord and tenant as obliged, and that the principles in force when the lease agreement is signed apply (s 6(1)). The Code of Conduct, renewal, permitted-deviation and Part 4 material is supported but is considerable padding.

Correctly says a landlord or tenant under a qualifying lease may complain, filed with an authorised dispute resolution body (s 9(1), defined by reference to s 10(1)). The detailed s 9(2)-(4) filing requirements are supported but go beyond what was asked.
Correctly says the licensee may supply liquor only at the licensed premises specified in the licence (s 5(1)); the definition of licensed premises is supported.

Correctly answers yes: s 8(4) lets the Licensing Officer impose any restrictions and conditions he or she thinks fit on grant or renewal. The s 8(5)-(6) variation power and s 8(2) refusal grounds are supported but extra.

Correctly answers yes: s 4(1) requires a common seal that may be broken, changed, altered or made anew as the Agency thinks fit. The additions on s 3 and the s 4(3) signing rule are supported but not asked for.
Correctly says the Minister specifies the member's conditions and term in the appointment, not exceeding 3 years (s 7(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly says the Board must have a common seal and that the Board itself decides its custody (s 4(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly says the Board may acquire by purchase, exchange or gift any object it considers desirable for its collections (s 15(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly answers no: s 10(4) bars a subdelegate from further delegating. The remark that s 10(2) permits subdelegation by certain delegates but not onward delegation is consistent with the text.
Correctly says copies of the annual and supplementary estimates go to the Minister without delay upon adoption by the Board (s 18(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.
Correctly answers yes: s 10(1) expressly covers "wilfully or negligently" destroying, damaging or defacing such objects, and s 10(3) gives a fine of up to $20,000.
Correctly says the Commissioner may issue or approve, and from time to time review and revise, such specifications (s 34(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.

Correctly states the s 11 guidelines cover conservation of buildings or land in a conservation area and protection of their setting, with the s 11(2) publication duty. The context bullets are mostly supported, but the claim that s 11 guidelines are the "relevant guidelines" a qualified person must comply with under s 24A is an inference not stated in the text, and the extras are distracting.
Correctly says planning permission is required for development of land outside a conservation area (s 12(1)); verbatim support in CTX1.

Correctly answers no: s 26(2) says the operation of s 24 is not an event of default. The additional detail on s 24, s 26(1), s 26(3) and s 25 is accurately drawn from the cited text but lengthy for the question.
Correctly says an arrested person may be detained until the name and address are correctly ascertained (s 28(2)); verbatim support in CTX1.

Both parts correct: the Minister must appoint a registered professional engineer as soon as practicable (s 8(4)), serving the remainder of the term (s 8(5)), and a person in Singapore may apply to the Board for recognition for overseas work with the prescribed fee (s 16). Supported by CTX1 and CTX2.

Gets the overseas recognition route right (s 16) but misses the second requested fact: licensed partnerships must report membership changes within 30 days (s 32(2)). The answer says no deadline appears in the extracts and points to an unrelated 30-day appeal period. It is honest about the gap, but long and padded with licence and revocation material.

Both parts correct: water prices follow prescribed tariffs (s 20(1)) and Board approval must be obtained before relocation or alteration works start (s 26(2)). The extensive s 20 and s 26 detail is supported but far beyond what was asked.

Both parts correct: the Board may refuse supply or a water installation while security is not given (s 22(2)), and approval of the projected water balance chart is needed before building works start (s 40(2)). The s 22(3)-(4) and s 40(3)-(4) details are supported.

Both parts correct: the Agency may appoint advisory or technical committees (s 5(1)) and licensees must provide a safe working environment so far as practicable (s 10(1)). However, the second claim is cited to [CITE:10], which is s 9 (registers of licences), not s 10 (CTX1); the content is supported but the citation is wrong.

Both parts correct: a licence application goes to the Director-General in the required form, with the prescribed fee and any required information (s 8(1)-(2)), and disposal of radioactive waste needs the Director-General's prior written approval (s 12(1)). The fine, imprisonment and disposal-definition details are supported.

Both parts correct: where part of a Government survey lot is affected the caveat must annex a plan identifying that part (s 8(3)-(4)), and a record of an official search result must be preserved at the Registry (s 20(1)). Supported by CTX1 and CTX2.

Both parts correct: an instrument must comply with the Act and rules before registration (s 17(2)), and the Registrar need not act on a fee-bearing matter without payment (s 28(1)). The extensive account of presentation, execution inquiry and s 13 conditions is accurate to the passages but is far more than asked.

Both parts correct: the Registrar must not complete registration of a contravening transfer (s 24(1)) and a housing developer must apply to the Controller before acquiring residential property (s 31(2)). The detailed s 24 procedure and s 31(3) conditions are supported, and it flags the missing s 31(4) text.

Both parts correct: the Controller determines the form and particulars of an application (s 25(3)) and the Minister appoints the Controller, who administers the Act subject to Ministerial directions (s 29(1)). Supported by CTX1 and CTX2.

Correctly states MCST's argument that it could reasonably rely on its independent contractor Zoe for a safe system of work, equipment and supervision, and separately and clearly reports the court's rejection under the WSHA (para [52]-[54]). One factual slip: it says Janaed fell from "a third chiller", whereas the text has him falling from Chiller 1 while the works were at Chiller 2. The breach framework and related submissions are supported but extra.

Correctly reports MCST's alternative positions: Zoe caused or contributed to the accident, and Janaed was 50% contributorily negligent (paras [11]-[14]). It clearly marks the 30% finding as the court's own holding; the s 15 Civil Law Act point is supported by CTX6.
Correctly says the claim was negligent misrepresentation against Mr Sim (the appellant), Faber and Ms Seah; supported by CTX1.

Correctly says the District Judge found only Faber liable and dismissed the claims against Mr Sim and Ms Seah. The additional points on Faber's breach, the High Court outcome and the Court of Appeal upholding Mr Sim's liability are supported by CTX3 and CTX12, with the roles of Mr Sim and Ms Seah from CTX1.

Correctly reports the 5-2 High Court of Australia finding that the defendant owed a duty to all the plaintiffs. The Court of Appeal's own view (no clear ratio, liability only to WF and possibly Rangara) is clearly attributed and supported by CTX4, but is extra.

Correctly states Spandeck laid down a single duty-of-care test regardless of the type of loss, and the three-stage test and proximity factors are supported by CTX1, 4, 6, 8, 13. The final claim cites [CITE:36], which is not among the retrieved passages; the point is otherwise supported by CTX8 and CTX1/6.

Correctly says the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal and held SSA not liable for the first flood, with breach, causation and costs supported. It misstates the pleadings point: CTX14 says the court found it unnecessary to rule on the High Court's inquiry duty, while the narrower duty comes from CTX18, so "because not raised in the pleaded cases" overstates. Much extra detail.
Reference requires breach; the answer gives breach and causation, both supported by the Court's statements (CTX4, CTX5, CTX9). Focused and accurate.

Correctly states that Animal Concerns shows personal liability is not precluded because the person is a director; the own-tort versus company-act distinction and the assumption-of-responsibility caveat are supported by CTX3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 15.

Correctly says the purchasers claimed in breach of contract and negligence; the third-party proceedings and Ng Sing/SGR Property outcomes are supported by CTX3, and the 2015 SGCA 15 description by CTX9.

Conveys that causation by the mops was not established but that the negligent handling brought it into the realm of probabilities (quote and res ipsa reasoning supported by CTX3; location point by CTX4).
Exactly matches the reference: the High Court in Virco held that nothing in the breach gave the first defendant a cause of action or defence; supported by CTX3.

Correctly states the question Caltex Oil addressed: recovery for economic loss caused by negligent damage to a third party's property. Facts and the exceptional-liability reasoning are supported by CTX3.

Matches the reference that the injury to the claimants was not foreseeable and direct, with the Weller facts (third parties' cattle, auction market closure) supported by CTX3; "indirect economic losses" is a mild paraphrase.
Correctly says the Court of Appeal held HAL and Lal Offshore did not owe a duty of care, with the alternative narrower duty also supported by CTX3.
Matches the reference: SSA alleged SRA was contributorily negligent for both floods by failing to seal the armoury windows despite earlier recommendations (CTX3).

The content of the reference is present: in Honeywill (recounted in [64]-[65]) the defendants argued the plaintiffs had no legal liability to pay as the defendants were independent contractors. But the answer opens by saying no passage records this contention and that it "falls outside the paragraphs supplied", which contradicts its own citation of CTX5. It also adds an unsupported "paid on advice" element to the argument and cites CTX2 for a referral to the judgment repository and a lawyer; much of the outcome section is off-topic.

Matches the reference: the second issue is the respondents' alleged liability for failing to exercise reasonable care in appointing the independent contractor ("negligent selection liability"). The personal/primary liability and standard-of-care/causation points are supported by CTX3 and CTX4.

Matches the reference: the live liability issue was the cause of the fire and the defendant's denial that its negligence caused it (CTX3). The broader issues and the finding that the fire began in Unit 141 are supported by CTX1 and CTX8.

Matches the reference: although the true cause was not established, the fire originated in the defendant's premises, which were under the control of its servants or agents (CTX3). The extra point about workers in occupation is also supported.

Gives the exact amount ($1,383,673.05) and the negligent servicing and maintenance of the fire hose reel system; every detail checked against CTX1, 2, 3 and 9 is supported. The outcome and causation discussion is extra to what was asked.

Matches the reference: the defendant relied on its contract with HDB (not with the plaintiffs) to deny a duty of care, and the court nonetheless found a duty. Supporting details are drawn from CTX1, 2, 3 and 7.

The main reason matches the reference: the Judge found NUS retained a very high degree of control over how Hydro worked (CTX12, CTX3). The closing paragraph on the Court of Appeal holding Hydro an independent contractor and the contract not showing control passed to NUS cites [CITE:32], which is not among the retrieved passages, and CTX14/19 do not state that holding; it is also extra to the question.

Gives both typical defences (deny negligence; assert independent-contractor status) as in the reference, supported by CTX5. The BNM illustration and the later NG HUAT SENG authority are supported by CTX4, 9, 12, 13 but are extra.

Correctly says the defendant argued it was not required to measure humidity, relying on the EMA checklist having no such requirement (CTX4), plus the equal-humidity argument (CTX3). The long section on why the argument failed is extra, and the decision date "2 June 2014" is not shown in the retrieved text.

Identifies the causation defence: that the Plaintiff's repeated refusal to conduct a shutdown maintenance was a novus actus interveniens, so the Defendant's negligence did not cause the flashover and it should not be liable. This matches the reference and is supported by CTX3, CTX13. The court's treatment, 70/30 apportionment and other detail are supported (CTX6, 11, 5, 8) but go beyond the question.

Correctly says the defendants owed lawful entrants a duty to take reasonable care for their safety (CTX3). However, the "what the duty required" bullets (warn of unusual dangers, qualified lifeguards, no duty re Oxyviva/AED) cite CTX6, where this is NUS's admission/contention, and present it as the court's holding; the answer is also long with much extra material.

The key statement, that pool operators have a duty to take reasonable care and responsibility for the safety of all who use their pools, is in CTX3 and matches the reference. The remaining six sections check out against CTX4-19 but are far more than the question asks.
Matches the reference: the Supreme Court of South Australia held the Crown did not owe the injured rider a duty of care, with the reasons given supported by CTX3.

Matches the reference: English courts had not definitively considered whether occupiers' liability should be subsumed under negligence. The statutory background is supported by CTX6; the parliamentary-supremacy point is plausible but the cited passage is cut off in the retrieved text.
Matches the reference: the District Judge held the management corporation 35% liable (CTX1). The 65%/75%-25% apportionment on appeal is consistent with CTX6, CTX7.

Matches the reference: the failure to establish a proper system was found to have caused the damage, shown through the DJ's "slightly better than 50% chance" reasoning and the High Court's "but for"/common-sense causation (CTX3, CTX4). The novus actus and 75/25 apportionment details are supported by CTX14 and CTX7.
Matches the reference: damages to be assessed by the Registrar, with interest and costs of assessment reserved to the Registrar (CTX5).
Matches the reference: Jones, the plaintiffs' third expert (a surveyor), did not testify because his evidence pertained to damages, which was not for the court's determination (CTX3).

Matches the reference: Henry and Keith JJ upheld the High Court's decision that the engineers owed the contractor no duty of care. The reasons given (risk allocation, no special skill/assumption of responsibility, departure from Edgeworth) are in CTX3.

Matches the reference: a duty of care to ensure the Geospecs Logs were accurate and reliable, breached through the negligent soil investigation and inaccurate logs (the particular breaches listed are in CTX1). The note that the claim failed for want of a duty (CTX13) is supported.

The answer correctly says the person could assume the carriage doors would be closed, but omits the other half of the reference (a duty is owed to people permitted on the platform). It also notes that the retrieved passage attributes the proposition to Hare v British Transport Commission, not Slater, which is accurate per CTX3 and flags a possible mislabel in the question/reference rather than answering confidently.

Matches the reference: SMRT and LTA owed the plaintiff a general duty of care in negligence to ensure she was reasonably safe at AMK Station; basis and proximity reasons are supported by CTX3 and CTX4.
Matches the reference: the Court of Appeal found no failure by the appellant to use reasonable care to prevent the damage; the 1986 state-of-knowledge reasoning is supported by CTX5.

The opening correctly says the defendant denied the negligence and occupier-liability allegations, matching the reference (CTX3). The very long remainder (legal framework, evidence, result) is supported by the cited passages but far exceeds the question.

Reaches the right answer ("No"): the earlier engine case (PT Bumi) did not allow the pure economic loss claim in tort against the subcontractor/engine supplier (CTX11, CTX12). It opens with a confusing statement that it could not find on-point authority, and the detail that the owner "deliberately" did not contract with the supplier is not clearly shown in the cited text.
Matches the reference: the buyer had only a contractual interest, not a proprietary or possessory interest, since property remained with the seller although risk was on the buyer (CTX4).
Matches the reference: the worker claimed damages for personal injury caused by, among other things, the defendants' negligence (CTX1); the note that no heads of damage are itemised is accurate.

The reference says the cause of action is characterised as negligence, with special rules for occupiers' liability. The answer opens by saying it found no direct authority, then calls it "negligence based on occupier's liability" owed to "trespassers". Nothing in the cited passage (CTX5) says the claimant was a trespasser (it describes a service engineer on the premises), so that part is unsupported, and the answer misses the "subject to special rules" characterisation.

Matches the reference: the District Judge found Hao Wei liable for not providing a safe system of work and not ensuring proper supervision (CTX2). The specific shortcomings (little instruction, no stopper, no warning, non-delegable duty) are supported by CTX3, 5, 7, 9.

Matches the reference: the duty to provide a safe system of work is non-delegable in a special sense, so performance may be delegated but liability is not escaped if it is not properly performed (CTX4, CTX13). The point about third-party sites is supported by CTX7.

Matches the reference: the patient won in the High Court because the doctor had not advised her to seek immediate medical attention (CTX2). The later reversal on causation and the liability-only stage are supported by CTX2 and CTX4.

Matches the reference: the trial judge relied on the contractual relationship between SME and Eric Ng (the Deed) to find proximity; the Court of Appeal's rejection is supported by CTX1, 3, 7, 9, 12. The label "Deed of Indemnity" does not appear in the retrieved passages, which refer only to "the Deed".

Matches the reference: principles for imposing a duty of care must be rational, coherent and capable of reliable and consistent determination; the fair-and-just, judicial-judgment point is from the same paragraph (CTX1).

Matches the reference: the trial judge found no duty of care to avoid causing pure economic loss (CTX1). The reasons (no direct contract, contractual recourse against the Employer, army camp) are from CTX4.
